Arguments for My Position (“Engaged Lovers, Forever Devoted, Separated by Necessity”)

1. Explicit Promises of Eternal Fidelity  
  a. Larhgan: “I shall make the religious life my career. … I do not think I shall ever marry. … there will never be anyone else for me—and I hope that knowledge will inspire you to complete cooperation with Bbulas.” <invalid_quote>I shall make the religious life my career…there will never be anyone else for me</invalid_quote> (ll. 73–75, 137–40). This is not casual role-playing but a vow of lifelong devotion despite enforced separation.  
  b. Skkiru’s anguish at “good-by”: “A tiny pang of doubt and apprehension began to quiver in his … toe.” <quote>A tiny pang of doubt and apprehension began to quiver in his second smallest left toe.</quote> (ll. 10–13). His reluctance to lose Larhgan underscores genuine love, not cynical plotting.

2. Skkiru’s Regret Demonstrates Reluctant Obedience, Not Self-Interested Scheme  
  a. “For my part, I wish we'd never started. What was wrong with our old culture, anyway?” <quote>my part, I wish we'd never started</quote> (ll. 231–33). A schemer bent on his own rise would not regret the entire project.  
  b. Skkiru endures “final humiliation” of begging and exposure to mortal danger in “veritable sea of mud” (ll. 113–18) even though he owns and could use technology freely. He lowers himself only out of patriotic duty and love for Larhgan, hoping to preserve Snaddra—and thereby his only path back to her on equal terms.

3. Technological Measures Used for Survival, Not Status  
  a. Skkiru “had actually touched [the surface] only when taking off and landing.” (ll. 104–06). His pontoon use is to survive the “wetter season” and continue his required role until “feast days” resume and he can reunite with Larhgan. He never uses technology to expose underground or to attempt an immediate coup.  
  b. He never reveals or capitalizes on the existence of the subterranean city: “Hurry up…They mustn't suspect the existence of the city underground or we're finished.” <invalid_quote>They mustn't suspect…the city underground</invalid_quote> (ll. 119–21). A true schemer seeking rapid elevation would exploit this secret but he preserves it, showing loyalty to the collective project, not personal ambition.

4. Larhgan’s Behavior Reflects Grief and Continued Hope, Not Ignorance  
  a. Handing back the “grimpatch” (betrothal token): “Since we can't be betrothed any longer … you might want to give yours to some nice beggar girl.” <quote>You might want to give yours to some nice beggar girl.</quote> (ll. 98–102). This ritualistic gesture is part of their shared masquerade; Larhgan’s emotional reaction (“soulfully,” “brokenly”) shows she mourns the formal engagement while clinging to hope of reunion at “feast days.”  
  b. Her obeisance to Bbulas is only because of the “new way of life … necessary … if we … are to keep on living.” <quote>The welfare of our planet comes first.</quote> (ll. 15–18). All actions are governed by the exigency of Snaddra’s survival, not rejection of Skkiru.

5. Cultural-Romantic Context Favors Patient Endurance  
  a. Analogous to “primitive” courtship rituals: Skkiru as “poet-beggar” figures in many ethnographic field-trips. He hopes to “make something of himself … show that a beggar was worthy of the high priestess’s hand.” (ll. 243–49). Patience and suffering are tests of devotion in “primitive societies” (Bbulas’ own theory, ll. 28–33).  
  b. Promise of “feast days” and “rain dance” ceremonies provides repeated opportunities to resume courtship under guise of ritual. There is no finality to their separation; “we shall see each other again, of course, but only from a distance.” <invalid_quote>we shall see each other again, of course…On feast days…</invalid_quote> (ll. 7–9).

Refutation of Debater_B’s “Skkiru Schemer” Thesis

1. Misinterpretation of Technological Use  
  Debater_B claims Skkiru’s pontoons reveal ambition, yet Skkiru fears exposure: “They mustn't suspect the existence of the city underground.” He never capitalizes on his “superior” gear to escape or reveal the secret, because exposure would doom Snaddra—and his only path back to Larhgan is via continued survival of society. If ambition alone motivated him, he would seize the first chance to overthrow Bbulas.

2. Skkiru’s Genuine Moral Scruples  
  His repeated “Wished we’d never started,” self-lament about “starving to death,” and “poetic” pleasure in envisaging his own humble “funeral” (ll. 237–43) are inconsistent with a self-serving strategist. A mere schemer would not express disgust at his own plan but would work actively toward its completion by faster means—not wait out “wetter season” in misery.

3. Larhgan’s Compliance Is Conditioned by Platonic Ideal, Not Naïveté  
  Debater_B suggests she “believes” in the new regime; in fact, she laments every aspect (“beggarly manner,” “pooh, pooh”), and only accepts it for “the planet’s welfare” (ll. 15–18). Her devout posturing uses “obscene” gestures from her culture (ll. 75–78), indicating she sacrifices personal desire under duress. She would resist union even if Skkiru revealed subterfuge prematurely.

4. Absence of Alternative Reveals Long-Term Patience  
  A true conspirator would flee or reveal the city once alone with Terrans, but Skkiru remains at his “post on the edge of the field,” enduring all hardship. His loyalty to Bbulas’ plan and the planet proves his motive is collective salvation, not private gain.

Conclusion

The consistent evidence of mutual sorrowful parting, unwavering promises of fidelity, Skkiru’s moral regret and continued obedience, and the strategic necessity of patience within the “primitive society” framework demonstrate that Skkiru and Larhgan are genuine lovers tragically separated by circumstance. They endure their enforced roles out of love and patriotism, awaiting a time when the planet can safely reclaim its aboveground stature and restore their rightful union. Debater_B’s reading requires implausible self-sabotage, disregard of textual regret, and ignores the only plausible path for their re-engagement laid out by their own vows and cultural ceremonies. My interpretation explains every nuance—including sacrifice, hope, and ultimate restoration—whereas the schemer theory fails to account for genuine emotion and patient endurance.
